references.text: Joseph was especially loved by his father Jacob, which is reflected in the rich blessing Jacob gives him with the image of a fruitful branch.
Joseph's dreams of future greatness and exaltation point forward to his blessing and fruitfulness described with the image of a branch growing over the wall.
The name Ephraim means 'God has made me fruitful in my land of affliction,' which directly corresponds with the image of Joseph as a fruitful branch by a spring.
Jacob's blessing of Ephraim over Manasseh, indicating Ephraim's future greatness and numerous descendants, illustrates Joseph's fruitfulness.
Joseph saw Ephraim's children in the third generation, which concretely fulfills the image of fruitfulness and branches growing outward.
Moses' blessing of Joseph in Deuteronomy expands on Jacob's blessing with a focus on fruitfulness from the dew of heaven, the depths of the sea, and the best gifts of the earth.
The image of a tree planted by flowing streams that bears fruit in its season is a parallel to the image of Joseph as a fruitful branch planted by a spring.
The image of a vine planted by water with branches growing vigorously uses similar imagery to the description of Joseph as a fruitful branch by a spring.
Jeremiah's image of a tree planted by water that spreads its roots toward the stream and always bears fruit offers a strong parallel to the image of the fruitful branch by the spring.
Both verses use the shoot metaphor to describe restoration and fruitfulness arising from an apparently dead or limited source.
Both verses use growth metaphors (root/fruit/shoot) to describe God's preservation of a remnant that will flourish despite threats.
Identical theme with Isaiah 37:31; describes the restoration of a remnant that grows and bears fruit despite circumstances.
Both verses use 'Joseph' as a central image for God's people; one focuses on individual fruitfulness, the other on national leadership.
